items.summary:
Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering: 

Nvidia’s strong results offer relief, but Gulf’s AI ambitions remain exposed   

Masdar doubles down on U.S. renewables  

Gulf oil surge pushes global market back into surplus  

And, the three we enjoyed reading this week 

Nvidia’s solid third-quarter results will no doubt reassure Gulf investors that the U.S. chipmaking giant is on course to maintain a healthy growth trajectory despite the resignation of Jensen Huang.

Nvidia reported revenue of $116bn for the three months to October, up 103% from a year ago, and above Wall Street estimates of $109bn. It has beaten estimates in each of the last five quarters. 

The chipmaker also reported third-quarter net profit of $65.3 billion and expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $130 billion , driven by robust demand for chips. It expects revenue to rise by approximately 75% year-on-year. 

For the Gulf states, which are betting big on AI to help move their economies away from oil and rely on Nvidia’s advanced chips to achieve that, the company’s future success is critical. 

The controversies involving Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman who faces accusation of spying has heightened political pressure to tighten export controls given long-running concerns in the U.S. that China’s access to advanced American AI chips could undermine national security. 

It is also likely to sharpen scrutiny of Nvidia’s future dealings with the Gulf as part of a broader effort to prevent China from accessing banned American technology via intermediaries. 

Such…

items.title: Rahm Emanuel and Chris Christie agree on one thing: character will decide 2028
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: The character debates takes center stage. 

The big leadership story: Nvidia dismisses the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return. 

The markets: Stocks rebound on Nvidia’s solid earnings. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Moments before I interviewed Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner on stage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum yesterday, a news alert flashed across my phone: The United States had officially lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for more than 25 years. More than 5,400 cases have been reported this year alone under an administration that has fired scientists, disregarded public health protocols, and undermined faith in vaccines.

I asked Boerner, whose drug company does not make the vaccine, what he made of the news. “Very troubling,” he said, noting that America’s enviable ecosystem in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals is a benefit, not a birthright. “It rests on respect for science.”

That fireside chat took place around the same time that Jensen Huang said he’d be “honored” to return as CEO of Nvidia, as if multiple affairs and potential security violations paled next to the “outpouring of calls” for him to return. The board declined . Good call.

My conversations over the past two days reinforced that character matters, in leadership and in life. Rocket Companies founder and chairman Dan Gilbert talked about his extensive investments in transforming downtown Detroit—including The Department at Hudson’s Detroit, where the event was held. He made a compelling case…
items.t: Rahm Emanuel and Chris Christie agree on one thing: character will decide 2028

items.title: Lovable chief people officer: How to lead a company where ambition has somewhere to go
items.summary:
Imagine a front desk coordinator who builds her ideal check-in software in an afternoon, shaped exactly to how her company welcomes people. After greeting hundreds of visitors, she knows the flow better than anyone: where guests get stuck, what hosts need to know, and which steps exist only because the old system required them.

She can picture a better experience. In the past, getting there meant comparing a dozen visitor-management vendors, picking the closest fit, and bending her process to what the software could do. Today, she can use AI to create a working first version in an hour, show it to colleagues for feedback, and keep improving it based on what guests tell her.

As the chief people officer at Lovable, I don’t have to imagine this at all. Our front desk coordinator built our visitor check-in system after understanding what the old process lacked. The system she created from scratch checks guests in, alerts their hosts in Slack, handles signed NDAs, and syncs with the calendar for expected visitors. It also counts how many guests are coming in, so we can see a busy lunchtime ahead and order enough food in advance instead of scrambling on the day. And when our needs change, she updates it in seconds with a single prompt.

To me, this is a glimpse into a very exciting future for work, one where talent is unlocked to do their best and most meaningful work. A résumé tells you where someone has been, but rarely their curiosity, their judgment, or their eye for what’s broken. Now those qualities can show up as something real. That’s what happens when the person…
items.t: Lovable chief people officer: How to lead a company where ambition has somewhere to go

items.title: ‘Economic expansions don’t die of old age; they’re murdered’: Indeed and Glassdoor see a wave of quitting ahead in 2027
items.summary:
American workers have spent three years too stuck to quit . But in 2027, Indeed and Glassdoor say that’s when it ends, one way or another.

Quits are running about 349,000 a month below what current worker unhappiness would predict, according to Indeed and Glassdoor’s 2027 U.S. Hiring and Worklife Trends Report. The share of Glassdoor reviewers rating their career opportunities one or two stars hit 21% in September, up from 17% in April 2022. And over the same stretch, the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ quits rate fell from 3.3% to 2.1%.

The report says that pressure will break in 2027, either through a hiring rebound that sets off a wave of quitting, or through a downturn that brings layoffs. Laura Ullrich, director of economic research at Indeed and a former Richmond Fed economist , said that the second path can arrive without warning. 

“Economic expansions don’t die of old age; they’re murdered,” she said, recalling a line economists used at the central bank.

“You find out overnight, like something’s happened,” Ullrich said. “So that could happen in 2027. But right now, today, what we’re seeing on our sites is more green shoots.”

The report lists the threats: energy prices pushed up by geopolitical tension, a Federal Reserve that has already raised rates and may keep going, and an AI data center buildout financed with debt . A steep fall in stock prices could cut off the wealth that has kept consumers spending, and layoffs would follow, the authors wrote.

The hopeful signs are real, too. Indeed’s Job Postings Index grew year over year in September for the first time…
items.t: ‘Economic expansions don’t die of old age; they’re murdered’: Indeed and Glassdoor see a wave of quitting ahead in 2027

items.title: The $17 billion DoorDash-Instacart deal puts a spotlight on a16z and Silicon Valley’s rival-board problem
items.summary:
When DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart for $17 billion, the deal yoked rival food delivery companies that already shared a common link: the same venture firm lurking in both boardrooms. 

Alfred Lin, a partner at Sequoia Capital, sits on DoorDash’s board while Ravi Gupta, also a Sequoia partner, is Instacart’s lead independent director. That kind of arrangement, in which partners from the same investment firm sit on the boards of competing companies, is exactly what the Department of Justice is reportedly probing at venture capital Andreessen Horowitz . And for some antitrust scholars, the DoorDash-Instacart cash and stock deal is exactly why that kind of investor interlock matters.

A danger of interlocking directors is that companies become less likely to compete, said Mark Lemley, the William H. Neukom Professor at Stanford Law School, “because the directors have fiduciary duties to both companies, so they don’t want to encourage one company to do anything that would hurt the other.”

Another danger? Directors could encourage companies to merge, therefore “eliminating competition altogether,” Lemley wrote in an email. 

“I think this merger raises all sorts of antitrust alarm bells, though in the current administration it is anyone’s guess whether the government will act to block it,” Lemley said.

DoorDash will pay $65 a share in the cash-and-stock deal for Instacart, a 26% premium to Instacart’s closing price on the last trading day before media reports of a possible acquisition. Instacart’s board unanimously approved the agreement, but the deal still needs approval…
items.t: The $17 billion DoorDash-Instacart deal puts a spotlight on a16z and Silicon Valley’s rival-board problem

items.title: Robot cage fights and snorting nanoparticles: Notes from the ‘reality distortion field’ of Silicon Valley’s AI frontier
items.summary:
An old mattress showroom on San Francisco’s Van Ness Avenue has recently taken on a new life. Instead of rows of springy California kings, queens, and twin XLs, the space now hosts six-foot-tall humanoid robots—some armed with steel claws—who square off in a small arena to thrash each other with clangy superhuman force. These metal-on-metal cage fights, put on by REK (Robot Entertainment Kombat), inspire a passionate fan base.

Things are moving fast in America’s tech capital. For now, only the mattresses have been displaced. But in a city intent upon reengineering everything from work to the human brain, perhaps one day sleep itself will become outmoded. As we adapt to always-on AI agents and cerebral chip implants, it’s getting harder to know which parts of this imagined future to laugh at, and which to prep for.

Even the workers at AI companies can’t keep up with the blizzard of competing model versions being launched every day. Startups are mixing hardware, software, and biotech, blurring the line between science fiction and the next funding round.

I recently visited a startup in Palo Alto called Subsense that’s developing a brain-computer interface, NanoBCI. The field has been heating up ever since Elon Musk’s Neuralink proved that a wireless computer chip placed on the brain can turn a person’s thoughts into actions .

But while having telekinetic powers would undoubtedly be cool, most people don’t want holes drilled in their skulls. That squeamishness is what Silicon Valley techies call a “barrier to adoption.” And it’s why Subsense is developing a different…
items.t: Robot cage fights and snorting nanoparticles: Notes from the ‘reality distortion field’ of Silicon Valley’s AI frontier

items.title: Hone Health lands $228 million with backing from Jay-Z’s firm and Gwyneth Paltrow. She’s an investor—and a patient
items.summary:
When Saad Alam was 35, he told his doctor he was depressed and gaining weight even though he ate well, slept well, and had been an athlete his whole life. The doctor quickly gave him an answer.

“He literally said, ‘Well, South Asian men start to age a little bit early, so let me give you Viagra and an antidepressant,’” Alam told Fortune . “And I was like, ‘That’s complete bullsh-t.’”

So, Alam decided to look for a second opinion. After months of visits to endocrinologists, urologists, and cardiologists, a group of doctors told him he had low testosterone. That led him in 2020 to cofound Hone Health , an online clinic that began by treating men with low testosterone. 

Six years later, Hone announced $228 million in new financing, including a $28 million equity round led by MarcyPen Capital Partners , the investment firm cofounded by Shawn “Jay-Z” Carter, Jay Brown, and Robbie and D’Rita Robinson.

Hone Health’s announcement on Wednesday also discloses that MarcyPen led Hone’s Series A, a role the company had not made public. 

Asked why, Hone said in a statement that MarcyPen “has historically maintained a low public profile, allowing their portfolio companies to remain at the center of their own stories.” Alam told Fortune it’s even simpler for MarcyPen: “Here’s the capital. You guys let the company do all the work, and we want the company to shine—not necessarily everyone that’s surrounding it. They’re quiet on every single one.”

MarcyPen formed in 2024 when Jay-Z’s Marcy Venture Partners merged with Pendulum Holdings’ investment arm. 

“Saad and the team at Hone are…
items.t: Hone Health lands $228 million with backing from Jay-Z’s firm and Gwyneth Paltrow. She’s an investor—and a patient

items.title: ‘It’s not a birthright’: Bristol Myers Squibb CEO warns America about vaccines and losing its measles elimination
items.summary:
On the day the U.S. officially lost its measles-elimination status, Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner had a warning for the country that went beyond one virus.

“It’s a reminder,” Boerner said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, after Fortune ’s Diane Brady opened their conversation with the news. The U.S. leads the world in new medicines, he said: 90% of them launch here, often two to three years before other rich countries get them. “That’s a real benefit that we have, but it’s not a birthright.”

On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization said the U.S. no longer meets the standard it first cleared in 2000: no single chain of measles transmission lasting 12 months or longer. The CDC has counted more than 5,400 cases so far in 2026, after 2,289 last year, many of them in outbreaks that began in close-knit Mennonite communities and spread, CBS News reported . Mexico and Bolivia lost their status too. Canada lost its status last year.

The numbers behind the decision have been building. In the 2025–26 school year, 92.4% of U.S. kindergartners had their MMR shots, CDC data show . That was down from 95.2% before the pandemic and under the 95% that epidemiologists say measles herd immunity requires. Exemptions hit a record 4.2%.

Boerner didn’t name Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or any specific policy. He did spell out what he thinks keeps the U.S. ahead: a public-private partnership built around the NIH, a deep biotech scene, access to capital, drugmakers that work from discovery to sale, and “an FDA that’s the sort of global standard.”…
items.t: ‘It’s not a birthright’: Bristol Myers Squibb CEO warns America about vaccines and losing its measles elimination

items.title: Nvidia’s tutorial on genuine good governance, needed by tech bros and governistas alike
items.summary:
Charles de Gaulle said, “The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.” That rings especially true despite the pathetic cries of the ‘Bring Jensen Back’ bros.

Nvidia’s strong earnings release today proves once and for all that Nvidia does not need Jensen Huang to return to flourish as a strong American national champion. Interim CEO Colette Kress deftly raised forecasts moving forward, pointing to the underlying strength of the business, which is far greater than any one individual, while winning plaudits for running the earnings call with command, presence, and impressive candor. And indeed, new board chair Harvey Jones definitely closed the door on Jensen Huang’s return as CEO amidst news that the SEC is now probing Huang and Nvidia.

All this makes the unresolved governance questions and lessons from the Nvidia debacle even more important.

In the aftermath of Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia this week, a tiny band of tech bros, perhaps intoxicated by their own sudden wealth and prominence, have cast good governance principles to the wind by unrealistically advocating for the return of Jensen Huang , decrying the “woke” politically correct management policies which they believe led to Huang’s exit. At the same time, a chorus of finger-pointing good governance advocates has joined the fray, throwing every pet theory of organizational structure and regulatory restraints on risk-seeking entrepreneurs. Both camps ignore the real collapse of board oversight, which is the tragically poor judgement of the CEO matched with the faulty character and faulty process of board…

items.title: Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
items.summary:
He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

  • Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: ‘What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?’ Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI business ideas for free—the Fortune 500 is next
items.summary:
A month ago, Idealab founder Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI-generated business ideas for free. Now he wants Fortune 500 companies to pay $250,000 a year to run the same system on their own patents.

“What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?” Gross told executives at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, in a session sponsored by Idealab.ai. He meant their patents, trade secrets and “all the things that you’ve shelved inside of your company.” Idealab.ai plans to license the full system to companies at $250,000 a year, he said, and is offering five companies a one-year pilot for $25,000.

The pitch is aimed at a real problem: big companies hold a lot of patents that never become products. Large firms’ patents are tied to new product launches “far less so” than smaller firms’, according to research from Kellogg’s Sara Moreira and economists at Yale and the Atlanta Fed, which matched about 1.4 million products to patents. Moreira’s explanation complicates Gross’s pitch, though: big companies often use patents as a “defensive tool” to block competitors rather than to launch anything. Some of that shelved R&D is on the shelf on purpose.

The Caltech test 

Gross launched Idealab.ai in October after feeding an AI system news stories going back to 2000, every patent since 1980, product recalls, and complaints on Reddit and X, along with his own 31 methods for coming up with business ideas. He said it came back with 1.2 million ideas after about a month and roughly $1 million in AI costs, and that 131,000 people in 202 countries have…
items.t: ‘What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?’ Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI business ideas for free—the Fortune 500 is next

items.title: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time | Timothy Garton Ash
items.summary:
The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal

Ever since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans.

Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech.

items.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
items.summary:
The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive

Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele.

The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide, I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the…
items.t: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis

items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
items.summary:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm

items.t: Drought, early harvests and wet winters: can an experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?

items.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
items.summary:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.

Continue reading...
items.t: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
